opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most important things, and it's something the field underestimated for a long time. Academic benchmarks for speech are useful, but they're very clean. You have read speech, studio-quality recordings, one speaker at a time, and you measure word error rate. Then you deploy and the real audio looks nothing like that. People call from a car with the window open, two people talk over each other, someone switches between French and English mid-sentence, there's hold music, there are domain-specific terms like drug names or product SKUs the model has never seen.

So our approach is to look at what customers actually send us and build evaluations from that distribution. When a customer says "it's not working well for us," we don't just tweak something and hope. We try to understand the failure: is it the acoustics, the accent, the vocabulary, the length of the audio, the turn-taking? Each of those becomes an eval set, and then we can track whether the next model actually gets better on it, rather than just moving a number on a public leaderboard.

The other thing real use cases teach you is that the metric itself often matters. Word error rate treats every word equally, but a customer in healthcare or finance cares far more about getting a name, a number, or a dosage right than about "uh" versus "um." For voice agents, latency and how the model handles interruptions can matter as much as raw accuracy. Listening to customers changes what you optimize for, not just what data you test on.

Of course, you have to be careful. You don't want to overfit to one big customer and degrade everyone else, and you have to respect privacy, so a lot of this is about understanding patterns and building representative test sets responsibly rather than training on whatever you receive. But in general, the gap between benchmark performance and real-world usefulness is where most of the work is, and the only way to close it is to stay very close to how people really use the models.

r001.rationale: The response proposes building evaluation sets from what customers actually send and tailoring them to specific failure types and audio conditions.

r002.rationale: It discusses tracking whether later models improve on customer-derived evaluations, but does not propose incorporating lessons from customer-specific improvements into the base model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I think the honest answer is that audio benchmarks lie to you much more than text benchmarks do, and real customer use cases are the only corrective we've found.

When we started on speech, we did what everyone does: you take LibriSpeech, you take Common Voice, you report word error rate, and you feel good because the number goes down. But the first time we put a model in front of an actual customer, a call center in France, say, or a company doing voice notes for field technicians, the gap was enormous. The audio is bad. There's cross-talk. People switch between French and English mid-sentence, they say product names that don't exist in any training corpus, and there's a truck going by in the background. None of that is in the benchmark.

So the first thing it changed for us is what we measure. Word error rate on clean read speech is almost irrelevant. What matters is: does the downstream task succeed? If someone says a customer ID or a dosage or an address, getting that exactly right matters a thousand times more than getting "um" and "uh" right. So we moved toward entity-level accuracy, toward task completion, toward measuring on the actual distribution of noise, accents, and domain vocabulary that customers see. We built internal eval sets from anonymized, consented customer-like data, and honestly, those are more valuable than any public benchmark.

The second thing is latency and robustness as first-class metrics. A customer doing real-time transcription doesn't care if you're one point better on WER if you take four seconds to respond. So we evaluate the model under the conditions it will actually be deployed: streaming, on constrained hardware, with the audio codecs and sample rates people really use. That's not glamorous but it's where the product either works or doesn't.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that customer use cases tell you what to put into training, not just evaluation. Code-switching, for example. We would never have prioritized it from the academic literature alone, but it's everywhere in real European and Indian audio. Same with multi-speaker diarization, same with handling domain jargon. The feedback loop is: customer fails, you figure out why, you build a targeted eval for that failure, and then you go fix the data. The eval comes before the fix. Otherwise you don't know if you fixed it.

The one caveat I'd give is that you can't just chase every customer complaint, because then you overfit to the three loudest customers. So we try to cluster the failures and ask: is this a category of problem that generalizes? Noisy audio is a category. Code-switching is a category. One customer's proprietary acronyms are not, and that's something they should solve with fine-tuning or a vocabulary bias, not something we should bake into the base model.

So, in short: use the real use cases to define what "good" means, build evals from them before you train, and let the frequency of failures across customers, not the volume of a single customer, decide the roadmap.

r001.rationale: It proposes internal evaluation sets based on customer-like data and measuring performance on the actual noise, accents, vocabulary, and deployment conditions customers encounter.

r002.rationale: It says customer use cases should guide training and proposes fixing data for recurring failure categories, but does not clearly state that lessons from customer-specific improvements should be incorporated into the base model. It explicitly excludes proprietary acronyms from the base model.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what the customer is actually trying to do. If they’re transcribing a conversation, if they’re building a voice assistant, or if they’re extracting information from a call, those are different problems. A single score on an audio benchmark won’t tell you whether the model is useful for all of them.

You want the evaluation to reflect the conditions they encounter: background noise, people interrupting each other, different accents, specialized vocabulary. And you need to understand which mistakes matter. Getting one word wrong might be harmless, but if that word is a name or a number that drives an action, it can be a big problem.

So I would make it a feedback loop. Look at failures in actual usage, turn those into representative evaluation cases, improve the model, and check whether that improves the customer’s task. For a voice assistant, that also includes latency—an answer can be correct and still arrive too late to make the conversation work.

r001.rationale: It says evaluation should reflect the customer’s specific task and conditions, and calls for representative evaluation cases based on real usage failures.

r002.rationale: It proposes using customer failures to improve the model, but does not say to incorporate lessons from those improvements into the base model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start from what the customer is actually trying to do. If they’re transcribing a conversation, recognizing the words is important, but so is knowing who is speaking, handling interruptions, and getting names right. If they’re building a voice assistant, latency becomes part of quality. A very accurate answer that arrives too late may not be useful.

So I would take representative examples from those workflows and build evaluations around them. Then, when the model fails, you can ask: Is this a problem with background noise, a particular accent, or specialized vocabulary? That gives you a much more concrete direction for improving the data or the model.

You still need general benchmarks, but the important thing is to check that improving a benchmark actually improves the customer’s experience.

r001.rationale: It proposes using representative examples from customer workflows to build evaluations tailored to those use cases.

r002.rationale: It discusses using observed failures to guide data or model improvements, but does not propose incorporating customer-specific improvements into the base model.
